idiom_name: Proc, lambda or Method objects as commands (call); a two-method object when undo is required
implementation_notes: Ruby's blocks, procs, lambdas and Method objects are first-class callables: Proc#call (with [] as an alias) or Method#call is the entire Command interface, and a Method object already carries its receiver, so the classic class hierarchy is unnecessary for plain commands. A history is an Array of callables driven with each(&:call), Symbol#to_proc covers the trivial cases, and the minimum structure for reversible edits is an object exposing call plus undo - the point at which a small class becomes worthwhile.
code_sketch:
class InsertText
  def initialize(doc, text) = (@doc, @text = doc, text)
  def call = @doc.insert(@text)                 # callable object is the command
  def undo = @doc.delete_last(@text.length)
end

history = [method(:save_document), -> { doc.insert("x") }]
history.each(&:call)                            # invoker
history.pop.undo
pitfalls: Proc and lambda semantics differ - return inside a proc returns from the enclosing method and arity is not enforced - so use lambda or -> for commands and let a wrong arity fail loudly.
Blocks and procs close over self and the surrounding locals, keeping the whole object graph alive for as long as the history holds them.
A Method object pins its receiver: replaying it later still targets the old object, so long-lived or persisted commands should carry an identifier instead of the bound method.
